stage_b_reviewed_content.statement:
Integral and finite morphisms of algebraic spaces are defined through scheme-base-change tests, with integral or finite property imposed on the representing scheme morphism.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a representable
morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$. Then
$f$ is integral, resp.\ finite
(in the sense of Section \ref{section-representable}),
if and only if for all affine schemes $Z$
and morphisms $Z \to Y$ the scheme $X \times_Y Z$ is affine and
integral, resp.\ finite, over $Z$.
hypotheses:
Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a representable
morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$.
conclusions:
$f$ is integral, resp.\ finite
(in the sense of Section \ref{section-representable}),
if and only if for all affine schemes $Z$
and morphisms $Z \to Y$ the scheme $X \times_Y Z$ is affine and
integral, resp.\ finite, over $Z$.

reason: Representable integral or finite morphisms are characterized by affine scheme-base-change tests exactly as in the scheme definitions; the cited scheme definition supplies both directions.

stage_b_reviewed_content.statement:
Integral and finite morphisms of algebraic spaces are defined through scheme-base-change tests, with integral or finite property imposed on the representing scheme morphism.

Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$.
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is representable and integral (resp.\ finite),
\item $f$ is integral (resp.\ finite),
\item there exists a scheme $V$ and a surjective \'etale morphism
$V \to Y$ such that $V \times_Y X \to V$ is integral (resp. finite), and
\item there exists a Zariski covering $Y = \bigcup Y_i$ such that
each of the morphisms $f^{-1}(Y_i) \to Y_i$ is integral (resp.\ finite).
\end{enumerate}
hypotheses:
Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$.
conclusions:
there exists a scheme $V$ and a surjective \'etale morphism
$V \to Y$ such that $V \times_Y X \to V$ is integral (resp. finite), and

there exists a Zariski covering $Y = \bigcup Y_i$ such that
each of the morphisms $f^{-1}(Y_i) \to Y_i$ is integral (resp.\ finite).

reason: Integral/finite conditions persist under étale base change. A surjective étale target scheme presentation with an integral/finite base change makes the total space a scheme and descends the condition effectively; Zariski locality yields the other equivalences.

Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$.
The following are equivalent
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is integral, and
\item $f$ is affine and universally closed.
\end{enumerate}
hypotheses:
Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$.

reason: Both integral and affine universally closed properties are representable and checkable after affine scheme base change, where the standard scheme lemma proves their equivalence.

conclusions: A finite morphism of algebraic spaces is quasi-finite.

reason: Finite morphisms are representable and may be tested after affine scheme base change; there a finite scheme map is quasi-finite by the scheme theorem, so the algebraic-space map is quasi-finite.

\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is finite, and
\item $f$ is affine and proper.
\end{enumerate}
hypotheses:
Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over
$S$.

reason: After arbitrary affine scheme-base-change, both finite and affine proper properties become scheme properties and are equivalent by the cited scheme lemma; étale-local descent gives the algebraic-space result.

Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $X_i \to Y$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$ be finite morphisms of
algebraic spaces over $S$.
Then $X_1 \amalg \ldots \amalg X_n \to Y$ is finite too.
hypotheses:
Let $S$ be a scheme.
Let $X_i \to Y$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$ be finite morphisms of
algebraic spaces over $S$.

reason: Finite disjoint unions of finite morphisms are finite by the scheme result; étale localization of the target and effective descent transfer the result to algebraic spaces.
